title: Accelerating variational quantum Monte Carlo using the variational quantum eigensolver
abstract_summary: The paper proposes quantum-enhanced variational Monte Carlo (QEVMC), which uses samples produced by variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) states as the initial distribution for classical VMC to accelerate convergence. The authors demonstrate—via numerical simulations and experiments on quantum hardware—that VQE-derived initial samples can speed up mixing to the target distribution, reduce the final energy relative to the raw VQE state, and be used from small quantum devices to aid larger classical VMC tasks, validated on the Fermi–Hubbard model (Gutzwiller ansatz) and the transverse-field Ising model (neural-network quantum states).
methodology_description: The authors propose and evaluate quantum-enhanced variational Monte Carlo (QEVMC), a hybrid workflow that replaces the classical VMC initial sampling distribution with samples produced by a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) (or other quantum procedure) and then runs a standard VMC pipeline unchanged. They give a theoretical motivation based on mixing-time bounds (χ2-divergence and fidelity between distributions) and implement and evaluate the approach on two benchmark many-body models: the Fermi–Hubbard model using a Gutzwiller variational ansatz, and the transverse-field Ising (TFI) model using neural-network quantum states (NQS). The experimental methodology comprises (a) generating VQE output distributions either by classical simulation or using previously published quantum-hardware runs (with postselection and symmetry averaging), (b) storing those samples and using them offline as the initial distribution D0 for Metropolis–Hastings MCMC inside VMC, and (c) comparing convergence to the target variational distribution (and to energies) against classical baselines (Slater determinant for Hubbard, uniform distribution for TFI). For the Hubbard model they use a local electron-hop proposal (flip neighboring pair 01↔10 within a spin sector); for the TFI model they use single-spin-flip proposals. They measure total variation distance to the target distribution, local-energy estimates, acceptance rates, and define speedup as the ratio of MCMC steps needed to reach a given TVD or energy error when starting from the classical baseline versus starting from VQE samples. Additional experiments include using small-system VQE samples concatenated to form initial states for larger-system VMC runs, and testing the effect of VMC on reducing VQE energy. For the NQS ansatz they optimize weights with stochastic reconfiguration (SR), use fixed numbers of MCMC samples per SR iteration, and compare different VQE layer depths (Hamiltonian variational ansatz) and NQS hidden-layer sizes.
experimental_setup: Evaluation combined (i) classical exact numerical simulations for small instances, (ii) use of previously published experimental VQE output distributions from quantum hardware (reference [24]) with error mitigation via postselection on occupation number and averaging over time-reversal/reflection symmetries, and (iii) classical VMC implementations. For Fermi–Hubbard experiments: system instances studied included 1x4, 1x8, 2x4 (small, accessible to exact simulation and hardware), and larger 1xL chains (L in {16,24,48}) created by concatenating independent 1x8 VQE samples to form initial states for larger VMC runs. For TFI (Ising) experiments: system sizes studied included N in {16,24,40,80}; VQE used the Hamiltonian variational ansatz with up to 4 layers (each layer with three parameters corresponding to even ZZ, odd ZZ and transverse-field terms), optimized with BFGS; NQS used one hidden layer with M = αN nodes (α in {1,2,4}); SR used 200–300 iterations; sampling used MCMC with single-spin-flip proposals and typical sample sizes of 5,000 per estimate. Exact stochastic-matrix multiplications were used on small systems to compute TVD; for larger sizes standard VMC sampling was used.

overall_pipeline: Generate or obtain VQE output samples (either via classical simulation of ansatz or from experimental runs).
Store these samples offline and use them as the initial distribution D0 for VMC runs.

Run Metropolis–Hastings MCMC to sample from the target variational distribution p_theta (given by amplitudes of the chosen ansatz). At each proposed move compute acceptance probability = min(1, p_theta(y)P(y→x)/(p_theta(x)P(x→y))).
For Hubbard: use Gutzwiller ansatz amplitudes (evaluated classically) with electron-hop proposals (neighbor flips). For TFI: use NQS amplitudes with single-spin-flip proposals.
Measure convergence using total variation distance (TVD) to target distribution when available (small systems via exact distribution) and local-energy estimates (averaging Eloc(S) over samples).

Define and compute speedup factor as the ratio of MCMC chain lengths required to reach a target TVD or energy error when starting from the classical baseline (Slater determinant or uniform) versus starting from VQE samples.

For NQS training (SR): run stochastic reconfiguration iterations using MCMC sampling (e.g., 5,000 samples per iteration, chain length per sample 15–20 for small sizes), compare convergence when initializing MCMC from uniform vs VQE distributions.
Explore concatenation strategy to use small-system VQE samples as initial states for larger-system VMC.

key_findings: [supported] Replacing the classical VMC initial distribution with samples produced by VQE (quantum-enhanced VMC, QEVMC) can accelerate convergence to the target VMC distribution for the tested instances (Fermi–Hubbard and transverse-field Ising models).
[supported] In several tested cases, running VMC starting from VQE samples produced final-state energies lower than the energy of the raw VQE state (observed for some Fermi–Hubbard instances).

[supported] VQE samples generated on small quantum devices can be reused (via concatenation of independent samples) as initial distributions to accelerate VMC for larger-system instances beyond the quantum device capacity (demonstrated in simulations for larger 1×L Fermi–Hubbard and larger TFI instances).

[supported] Empirical measurements in the paper show substantial runtime speedups (reduction in required MCMC steps) in multiple experiments/simulations relative to standard classical initializations.

[supported] The observed QEVMC speedup appears to come from the VQE-produced initial distribution being closer to the target distribution (not from a higher Metropolis acceptance rate); acceptance rates were equal or lower when starting from VQE samples.

[speculative] A theoretical argument using χ^2-divergence and fidelity links higher fidelity of the VQE initial state to smaller χ^2-divergence and hence fewer MCMC steps; this provides intuition (but not a general proof) for why QEVMC can reduce mixing time.

[speculative] QEVMC is expected to be robust to noisy quantum states and may even benefit from some noise (authors argue small noise interpolates between perfect VQE and uniform classical input and could reduce distance to target).
[supported] QEVMC requires only offline (noninteractive) access to a quantum device: a single batch of samples can be stored and used by classical VMC without further quantum operations.

[speculative] QEVMC offers a practical path for near-term noisy quantum hardware to assist classical algorithms even when the device cannot prepare high-fidelity ground states; broader practical advantage remains to be established.
results_summary: The paper introduces quantum-enhanced variational Monte Carlo (QEVMC), where VQE-generated samples replace the usual classical initial distribution for VMC. Using numerical simulations and some experimental data on small quantum hardware, the authors show that starting VMC from VQE samples can (in many tested cases) reduce the number of MCMC steps needed to reach the target distribution, sometimes lower the final VMC energy compared to the raw VQE energy, and allow small-device VQE samples to accelerate VMC on larger systems via concatenation. The authors provide empirical speedups on specific Fermi–Hubbard and transverse-field Ising instances and present theoretical intuition (via χ^2-divergence and fidelity) linking initial-state fidelity to mixing time. They emphasize QEVMC's simplicity (offline sampling) and anticipated resilience to noise, while noting that observed advantages are instance-specific and not proven to imply asymptotic quantum advantage.
performance_claims: [supported] Up to 14× speedup (reduction in required Metropolis steps) observed for simulated 1×8 Fermi–Hubbard instance when using VQE initial distribution versus Slater-determinant initialization.
[supported] Up to 6× speedup observed for the 1×4 Fermi–Hubbard instance using experimental VQE samples.
[supported] Little or no speedup observed in some experimental cases (notably some 1×8 and 2×4 experimental runs), indicating variability dependent on instance and experimental noise.

[supported] For transverse-field Ising (TFI) tests: up to 20× speedup reported for a 16-spin instance using a 4-layer VQE state; up to 46× speedup reported for a 24-spin instance using a 1-layer VQE state (relative to uniform initialization).

[supported] Concatenation of 1×8 VQE samples was used to accelerate VMC on larger Fermi–Hubbard chains (1×16, 1×24, 1×48) in simulation, with faster convergence of energy in several cases; in particular, for 1×48 the experimental VQE-derived concatenated distribution gave the fastest convergence among tested starts.
[supported] Reported VQE energies for experimental Fermi–Hubbard runs: −3.37 (1×8) and −3.71 (2×4) (quoted as the energies of the experimental VQE distributions in the paper).

[supported] Typical sampling parameters used in reported experiments/simulations include chains and sample sizes such as 5000 samples per energy estimate and chain lengths varied per experiment (figures detail specific chain lengths).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports empirical speedups on small, specific problem instances and provides theoretical intuition linking initial-state fidelity to faster MCMC mixing, but it does not prove an asymptotic or general quantum advantage. Observed benefits are instance-dependent, sometimes absent experimentally, and scalability/robustness to larger, practical problems remains unproven; therefore any claimed advantage is currently speculative.
limitations: Current quantum hardware is unable to run VQE on instances beyond the capacity of classical exact diagonalisation, limiting demonstrations to small / proof-of-principle problems.
QEVMC requires VQE-produced initial samples to have sufficient fidelity with the target distribution; low fidelity implies large χ2-divergence and long mixing times.
For large system sizes the total variation distance to the desired distribution is not accessible, making it unclear how observed effects translate to other observables or metrics.
Experimental VQE samples do not always produce a speedup (e.g. some 1×8 and 2×4 experimental cases), indicating sensitivity to noise, circuit depth and experimental imperfections.
QEVMC provides an initialization advantage but does not increase the MCMC acceptance rate; speedups stem from starting closer to the target, so benefits are limited to initialization quality.
Theoretical bounds (e.g. those based on χ2-divergence) provide intuition but not tight practical guarantees on speedups; actual speedups may be better or worse.
Methods that in principle converge to the true ground state still generally require exponential time; QEVMC does not evade the fundamental exponential hardness in the worst case.
[inferred] Demonstrations are limited to two canonical models (Fermi-Hubbard and transverse-field Ising); generality to a wide range of Hamiltonians and ansätze remains unproven.
[inferred] The approach assumes the VMC ansatz allows efficient evaluation of amplitudes (up to normalization); this may not hold for all useful ansätze.
[inferred] Concatenating / stitching small-system VQE samples to construct initial distributions for larger systems may neglect inter-block correlations and thereby limit effectiveness.
[inferred] Storing and using large numbers of offline quantum samples may incur practical resource / storage costs and impose engineering trade-offs not analysed in the paper.
[inferred] The performance benefit is contingent on the choice of mixer and MCMC design; whether other mixers would change results is not explored.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Proposes QEVMC: use VQE-produced samples as the initial distribution D0 for classical VMC (Metropolis–Hastings) to accelerate convergence without changing the VMC pipeline.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Demonstrates (via numerical simulation and previously published hardware samples) speedups in mixing to the target variational distribution and reductions in final energy when starting VMC from VQE samples versus classical baselines.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Validates approach with small-scale VQE experimental outputs (postselected and symmetry-averaged) and shows utility of small quantum devices as sources of useful initial samples for larger classical VMC tasks (including concatenation of small-system VQE samples to build larger initial states).
#idea:hybrid-approach — Shows that VMC can further reduce energy of raw VQE states, suggesting a complementary workflow where noisy NISQ outputs seed classical refinement.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Provides quantitative metrics (TVD to target distribution, local-energy estimates, acceptance rates, and defined speedup ratios) on benchmark many-body models (Fermi–Hubbard and transverse-field Ising) across multiple system sizes and ansatz choices.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Uses classical simulation, exact distribution computations for small systems, and experimentally obtained VQE sample sets (with postselection/symmetry averaging) to support practical applicability on current devices.
